If you're selling, I'll buy.
You're not going to ask where it came from?
You wouldn't tell me anyway.
Ha. Fair.
The bracelet goes into a wooden box under the counter. The lid snaps shut.
You cut the price like it was nothing.
I thought you'd at least pretend to hesitate.
Fine. It's yours now.
Has a girl come by lately? Selling something?
Upper-level accent, sharp tongue, about this tall, face longer than the shelves.
Yes.
She actually came.
We grew up together. As soon as her mother got into trouble, my family wouldn't even let me mention her name.
I called her. Told her to come stay at my place.
She answered with two words: no need. Then hung up.
I was so mad I didn't sleep half the night. Next day I still texted her.
She didn't answer a single one.
I'm not here to gossip.
I just want to know if she's been eating.
Leave the bracelet with you for now.
I'll come redeem it in a few days.
The scale's still out on the counter when she appears in the doorway.
Let me ask one thing first.
Lydia was here, wasn't she.
She runs a fingertip along the counter edge and sniffs it.
Her scent's still on the counter.
Did she pull out a bracelet?
Took it.
That was her best one.
The bracelet. She'd give up even that.
You didn't hide it from me.
That thing with the box last time—you told me about it later too.
You made up for it. I'll remember this time.
She pulled her hand back from the counter and stood straight.
Even what she said, you make me go ask her myself.
I asked. She said she found me a job.
The condition is I can't mention my mother's case.
I turned it down. Those were my own words.
She stopped talking after that, her hand still on the counter edge.
She told you about the job too, right? Upper levels. Good money.
The condition is I can't mention my mother's case again.
I turned her down to her face.
She argued for half an hour.
She's decent. Just loves arranging my life for me.
I'm saving money. Myself.
I've got the junkyard figured out. One look and I know which scrap pile's worth something.
You pay me the going rate for what I pick. That's help enough.
Don't give me extra. Short me and I'll say so.
So I'll keep coming.
That's it. Don't say anything else.
She straightened a crooked old casing on the counter, then turned.
I'll bring a new batch tomorrow.
She pushed the door open and went out, half a step slower than when she came in.
Eleanor comes to the window without speaking first.
Yesterday afternoon, a woman left through this alley.
Curly hair, new bag, doesn't watch where she walks.
What did she want.
To sell something.
Sell what.
A bracelet.
...She even brought that out.
It's an old family piece. Her mother wore it.
Did she ask you a pile of questions too?
Yes.
One trip down here, and she can go home saying she's seen me.
...Never mind. She's not a bad person.
She just doesn't know what it's like down here.
She rests her hand on the counter edge, fingertips scraping off a patch of old paint.
She came.
That's it?
...Right. There's nothing for you two to talk about.
People like her praise your stock when they arrive and forget it the moment they leave.
Do I know her?
You do ask.
Curly hair, new bag. Ten of those pass through this street a day.
Her hand stops on the counter edge and stays there.
...I know her. Her name is Lydia.
Did she mention me.
She did.
...What did she say.
That you haven't been eating.
How would she know whether I eat.
Twenty floors away, and she can count my meals?
She looks down at the notch in the counter.
...She doing all right.
Forget I asked.
The bracelet.
Under the counter.
Don't sell it.
...I mean, don't sell it to anyone else.
She'll come back for it. Lose something once, and she'll talk about it for half a year.
Don't tell her where I live.
She didn't ask.
She will.
Across from the ration station, fourth floor, no light in the stairwell.
If she really stood in that doorway, I couldn't even ask her in.
She sets the bag from her back onto the counter. It falls open, showing bits of shell and loose thread.
Will you take these.
I can't be bothered to haggle today.
The visitor stops at the window and looks around the shop through it.
Heard you took in an old bracelet a few days ago.
The wooden box goes onto the counter. The lid comes open.
Engraving inside the band.
Old engraved pieces from upstairs—you see two a year, if that.
It's all machine-stamped now. Hand-carved work like this — I know it.
Who was the seller?
Not your business.
One thousand.
Cash. Settled now. The money's right here.
A thousand. Not a credit more. If you won't sell, I'm gone.
Not selling.
It's in your hands. Your call.
Not today, and this price won't be here another day.
He pushes the box back half an inch and turns away from the window.
The box is pushed over. The broker counts the money slowly.
Pleasure.
If you get more like this, come to me first.
He wraps the bracelet in cloth and leaves without looking back.
She comes to the window with a stack of money in her hand and stays standing.
I'd like to get that bracelet back. Would five hundred do?
I can manage that much. Don't turn your nose up at it.
The bracelet is pushed over. Only the original amount is taken.
I counted out five hundred and everything. You…
Then I'm really taking the extra back.
Free?
...Don't look at me like that.
All right. I'll take it.
But I'll remember.
She takes the bracelet and says nothing more.
If I go too low, will you think I'm taking advantage of you?
...Five hundred. That's it. Don't make me raise it.
This bracelet was my grandmother's.
My family reported it stolen last month.
I took it from the cabinet. I was in a hurry that day and just grabbed it.
Who knew my mother would insist on counting everything one by one and then report it stolen.
How am I supposed to tell her about the pawnshop.
She slips the bracelet onto her wrist, turns it twice, and fastens the clasp.
There.
How's Eleanor doing?
I went to see her twice and never even got a word in.
First time I waited downstairs two hours. Second time she shut the door in my face.
I stood at the stairwell, so dark I couldn't see the steps, and felt my way down.
She carries things with her. How does she even get up those stairs?
I can still ask around about things upstairs.
How do you want to help.
I'll go ask her again. Next time we come together.
Only if she's willing to come.
When she does, help me talk to her.
She pulls her bag strap onto her shoulder, steps away from the window, then looks back.
Then I'll go find her.
She pushes the money over and waits a moment before she gets the bracelet.
She drags the sack up below the window, leaving a dusty streak on the ground.
I've been to the one at the docks. The scale's crooked.
He weighs wire by the pound, then pulls two strands off the top and calls it loss.
I put it back in the bag right there and walked out.
She turns the sack upside down and shakes it out. Shells and connectors scatter on the counter, lined up in three rows by condition.
Left side works as is. Middle needs repair. Right side is shells only.
You quote a price. If it's wrong, I'll say so.
Two in the middle row are good.
Which two?
The shopkeeper slides two connectors into the left row. She bends close, nose almost touching the counter.
...The rust's on the outer ring. The inside's bright.
Fine. You're right this time.
The coins slide across. She unties the change pouch at her waist and pours the coins from the counter and the pouch together.
Quiet. I'm counting.
Seven hundred sixty... seven hundred eighty...
She flips the pouch over and pats it twice. The last few coins drop out, gray with scrapyard dust.
Eight hundred. Exactly.
The pendant?
Still around my neck. I took it out to look when I was two coins short.
Then I put it back.
The shopkeeper pulls a clean cloth from under the counter and sets it by her hand.
For wiping my hands? The dirt on my hands is none of your concern.
She picks up the cloth and wipes the dirt from between her fingers too.
The detective sees me tomorrow. I'll bring the money myself.
Don't follow me. If he sees someone with me, his price changes.
I didn't give him all the originals. I kept copies, and noted the time of every meeting.
Thank you. I'm going to find out who did this to my mother.
...Today I was going to say I finally don't have to keep running to your shop.
I didn't say I'd stop coming. Until it's cleared up, I still have to eat.
I can pay. But from now on, you listen to me.
Put the business terms in writing. Whether I take the loan is my decision.
Not just business.
Then no loan.
My mother didn't teach me to pay a debt with myself. That's not how it works down here either.
The money's done. I sold the rest of the goods to another buyer and took an advance on some short work.
Their price wasn't good. I'll have to work a few more days. But I'll manage.
I'll manage. I said I'd find my own way.
The last part of the shortfall, I was planning to cover with the locket.
It's been hanging on me doing nothing. Now I want it to help me find my mother.
I have. Price it like anything else.
She comes to the window and checks both ends of the alley, keeping one hand inside her coat.
The detective got it out.
(She pulls her hand out, pressing a thin disc flat in her palm) Lab data disc.
Drawers locked, cabinets sealed. This was shoved under the lamp mount.
Mother's habit. She always said drawers are for other people to search.
Can you open it?
It needs a code. I tried all night.
Her work number, the farm number, my father's... everything I could think of.
Just before dawn, I typed in my own birthday.
It opened.
Something this important, and she used my birthday as the password.
What's on it.
A pile of records. Shifts, light cycles, materials, accounts. I don't understand half of it.
One I did understand. Nutrient fruit.
The kind the ration station hands out. No seeds. You know the ones?
I know. Seeds come when the top says so.
She made it seed again. Three rounds of retests. The seeds grow.
The lower districts could grow their own. No more holding out a hand every month.
There were letters in there too. From Pastel Company.
Each one politer than the last. All saying the same thing. Stop the research.
She answered the last one. Two lines. Said she wouldn't stop.
Two weeks later, that embezzlement shows up in the books.
Who else knows about this disc.
The detective. Me. Now you.
The detective took the money and left. Said it was too hot to touch.
The lock on my door is broken. People come to check out the room, in and out.
If I lose it at the dump, I'll never find it.
Anything else on the drive.
Yes. The workers' names, and a few accounts still open.
Leave it with me. There's a lock under the counter.
...I didn't ask you for anything.
(She presses her hand on the drive one more time before pushing it over) Just for a few days.
When I figure out what to do with it, I'll come get it.
I won't look. Won't touch it.
You said it. Don't go through it while I'm away.
I'll remember this.
She steps back and glances at the lock beneath the counter.
A man plants himself in front of the window, blocking it.
You get an Upper Tier girl in here a lot.
Lots of people come in to buy.
Don't play dumb. The one selling scrap. Her mother's in a cell.
She's got a drive. Came out of the lab.
Where'd you hear that.
The archive room door was opened. People saw.
I'm not looking for her. I'm looking for you.
Why me.
She won't talk to strangers, but she runs to your place every day.
You give her a message. Hand over the drive, her mother walks.
Case dropped, she's released. Simple as that.
You say let her go, and that's that?
Not me saying it. Someone else is. I just make the run.
(He digs a stack of money out of his coat and slaps it on the counter) Three hundred. Errand money.
You walk a few steps, open your mouth once, the money's yours.
If she won't hand it over...
It's cold in a cell. People get sick. Nobody finds it strange.
Get away.
(He pockets the money) I've said my piece. You won't take it to her, I'll go say it under her window myself.
Three days.
Take the money. I'll pass it on.
Not enough?
I'm not taking your money.
(He pockets the money) Your call. I'm not the one out three hundred.
I'll come back in three days for an answer.
The drive comes to you, I pick it up. Her mother gets word the same day.
Don't get any ideas about the Security Bureau. It's busier over there than you think.
You done?
Done. That girl's got a temper. Soften your tone when you talk her round.
If she won't listen, you're not the one who pays.
She comes to the window without a bag this time and first looks at the lock behind the counter.
You sent word for me. What's so important it has to be today?
Someone came by. They want that drive.
…Who.
A runner from the black market. Says if you hand over the disc, your mother gets out.
Out? They say out and she's out?
He says it's not his call. It's his boss's.
He gave me three hundred for the errand. I didn't take it.
Three hundred. That's what my mother's worth to them—one errand.
He also said the cells are cold. If someone gets sick, nobody would think twice.
(She grabs the edge of the counter)…He wouldn't dare.
They would. They made up the accounts. What wouldn't they do?
How many days did they give you?
Three days. Today's the second.
I didn't sleep at all last night.
If I hand it over, my mother might get out. The research goes back to Pastel, rotting in some drawer.
It's what she cares about most. She didn't stop even when it meant prison.
Don't hand it over—post it straight out, let the whole Lower District know the nutrient fruit can produce seeds…
Then while she's locked in there, she's the last card they can squeeze.
Hey, you. Tell me. I'm not asking you to decide for me—I just want to hear what move you'd make.
…Hand it over. Get her out first. The rest can wait.
Sophia's case dismissed. Subject released. Return to the Upper District prohibited.
The research is back in their hands. If she asks, I'll tell her myself.
First go to the Security Department and apply for protective custody. Move her out in the open.
Once she's protected, hand over the research—publicly.
The Security Department? They're the ones who locked her up.
It was that ledger that locked her up. Protective custody is a different form.
...But they did let me go in the end.
Her name's on the care form. If anything happens to her, someone has to sign and answer for it.
The detective's written statement is still there. He can testify the disc was taken from under the lamp stand and no one touched it.
I'll make a copy myself first. Before the original goes in, I'll get the contents into the public archive.
The disc's here. You want it now?
Now. (She takes it and clutches it in her palm.)
If that errand runner comes back, tell them I'm not handing it over. Don't say anything else.
And... you didn't take the three hundred.
Don't think I didn't hear.
Post it. Today. Make it so they can't cover it up.
Detainee Sofia died in custody. Cause under investigation.
...It's all posted. She's gone. Don't talk to me. I'll stand here a bit, then leave.
Detainee Sofia has been transferred to care. Case under review. Visitation by notice.
Lower District bulletin: hydroponic farm nutrient-fruit seed research has been placed in the public archive.
The notice is up. Did you see it?
Saw it.
I sat outside Security all day for that slip of paper.
The officer who signed it looked at the letter on the disc, and his face changed.
He said the review takes time. Didn't say how long.
Where is she?
She's safe. At least, that's what the form says.
Still no visits. They said wait for notice.
What are you buying?
Direct. Fine. I won't beat around the bush either.
(She doesn't sit, hand on the counter) Just tired. Same if I stand.
Sit.
...Just for a while.(She pulls up the stool outside the window and sits low)
After the research went up, everyone in line at the ration station was talking.
An older woman asked me if you can really grow your own. I said yes.
Then she asked if that meant no more nutrient fruit every day.
I said no. There'd only be more nutrient fruit. Her face fell right there.
Same as me.
What would your mother say if she knew?
She'd pick apart the copy I made and say my handwriting's crooked.
When I see her, I'll ask why she kept all of this from me.
I don't want nutrient fruit today. You got anything else to eat? Cheaper.
Sweet is fine too. Just for today.
Sweet. Half a month, and I finally get a bite that isn't that skin.
I'm going back to the junkyard tomorrow. That's it for today.
You undercharged. Don't think I can't tell.
…Just this once. Remember—next time I'll bring goods to make up for it.
That much for this little sweet? You're singling me out today.
Paid. Next time I'll check the price tags somewhere else first.
If you don't have any, forget it. I'll go back to nutrient fruit like always.
(She stands, steps back, then pauses) I'll come when there's news of the review.
The application's in. Still waiting for an answer.
You didn't tell me 'it's already fine.'
That's better, actually. People used to say 'don't worry' every time, and then I never saw them again.
I'm taking another short shift tonight. Waiting for news doesn't stop me eating.
I told my roommate that if anyone asks where my mother lives, not to say a word.
My roommate says I'm learning this late.
Your part is in the application too.
I checked your shop address twice.
Afraid that if something happens, I wouldn't be able to find you.
You're here. That's why I dared to take it this far.

The safety review for the person concerned has been accepted. Transfer to temporary protective custody approved; family may visit after verification. This measure does not mean the original case is dismissed.
I... I can see her?
All right. I'll go now. Verify first, then see her.
If it's real, I'll come back and tell you. In person.
Verify the person and the paperwork first. Don't just take a messenger's word that it's done.
I want my mother to confirm it herself. Someone else reading a line for her doesn't count.
No copy. If I'm trading it for her, I can't use her life as collateral and gamble that they won't find out.
I've thought it through. Whether there's another way later is a later problem.
Today, I just want to see her.
Still no confirmation that she can be released, right?
No. Keep applying, or switch to handing over the drive for her release.
I don't want to treat 'processing' as if she's already safe. Get her out first.
Hey! My mother is free!
I saw her myself! The first thing she asked was whether I'd been skipping meals again.
She was exiled to the lower levels. She can't go back to her old farm.
But we're together again. Tonight, I know where she's sleeping.
I saw Mother! She's been moved out, someone's watching over her, and the visit is registered.
She knows what comes next. The research, the threats, going public. I told her everything.
She said to let the protection staff confirm the arrangements first, then send the material out.
She said I'm reckless enough for both of us. Someone in the family has to ask more questions.
I had so much prepared: how she ate in there, why she didn't tell me sooner, whether anyone hurt her.
Not a single one. I just called her 'Mom'.
She said she heard me, and I didn't have to shout.
Now I can ask her slowly.
I used to think that as long as I could get back upstairs, everything would return to the way it was.
But today, when I saw her, I didn't even think about the house up there.
First I'll find a place to live down here. My roommate will help look, and I can keep working.
If I need anything, I'll buy it. At full price. You've done too much for us. I can't have you paying for everything from now on.
But today, I want to thank you properly, once.
All I could say then was that I wanted to save her. You helped me bring her home.

The research on restoring nutrifruit seeds has been handed to independent researchers for verification. The representative of Pastel's station office is suspected of coercion and interference in the case and is now under investigation.
The person concerned is currently under registered protection. The original embezzlement case is still under review; the investigation result does not constitute a final ruling.

The registered protection arrangements have been confirmed. The family is permitted to register a residence in the lower levels and live together, and may carry on normal daily activities. Contact person and address are on file; contact must be maintained during the review of the original case.
Hello. Eleanor says that when you buy things here, the owner tells you the flaws first.
She also said the owner isn't always good with words, but he's not a bad person.
I'd like some household goods, and something to eat. There's still a lot missing where we live.
She's off to work. Before she left, she told me not to lug home everything just because it's cheap.
I used to tell her the same thing, and she'd pretend not to hear.
She told me what you did for her.
But when she talks about herself, she says far less than when she talks about you.
Or maybe she's waiting for me to ask.
The research was returned. Of course that doesn't sit well with me.
But don't let her think bringing me back is something she has to apologize to me for.
The material has been sent out. I'll keep cooperating with the review. The rest will take time, step by step.
You were right to get me transferred before publishing. The people with the least protection shouldn't always be the ones paying the price.
That's all. Don't refuse to take my money just because it's me.
She won't take things for free. That part is certainly like me.
When she talks about this place lately, it's not just about what she bought.
And whatever else she said, go ask her yourself. I won't finish her sentences.
A woman comes to the window in a gray coat, a care-office registration badge on her chest.
Hello. East of the ration station, third shop window. This is it, right?
Eleanor drew me a map. More detail than the shift rota back at our farm.
This is it.
She says you sell things, and you tell the faults first.
I came for some daily goods. And to check that for myself.
Left shelf. Top two bottles. Lids don't screw on tight.
She goes to the left shelf, twists each of the two bottles in turn, puts them back, and takes the ones from the back row.
They really don't. You didn't lie to her.
Some nutrient fruit too. She drew a fruit on that map in the room.
She picks up a nutrient fruit, presses the skin with her thumb, and turns it half around under the lamp.
Ration station batches. Skin's dark. Hollow inside.
Anyone can look up the data now. The kind you can actually grow — nobody's handed out seedlings yet.
You're not going to do anything about it?
The review isn't closed. I have to stay at the registered address. The guard calls my name twice a day.
This morning a worker had the guard pass on a message. Asking if the next shift rotation is still on.
I can't answer. The research belongs to everyone now. My hands are empty.
Don't tell her that. She'll think it's her fault I lost my work.
She sets the things on the counter, digs a few credits out of her coat pocket, and lays them out one by one.
Did she tell you how she saved up those eight hundred credits?
Selling salvage. One deal at a time.
She used to barely look at price tags. She didn't tell me much about this.
That's the total.
Don't charge me less just because I'm wearing this coat.
She's been sleeping deep these days. Last night she talked in her sleep. Haggling with someone.
If she wants to come, she'll come herself. I'm just here to buy things.
She slips the nutrient fruits into her coat pocket, nods to the shopkeeper, and leaves.
Did my mother come by?
She did. Bought some things, paid for them. She told me to ask you.
I knew it.
Then don't ask today!
I brought some goods. This time I'm really here to sell.
My mother gets up earlier than I do now. Two days ago I woke up and found her sitting there repairing an old tray.
She says if her hands aren't doing something, she starts thinking about what happened in there.
I handed her the tools and sat with her for a while.
Nothing special. I just sat there for a while.
I always thought that once she was out, I'd know what to do next.
Work continues, the room needs tidying, meals have to be made. I know all that.
It's just... I don't need to invent a reason to come here so I can ask you for help.
You said that. Remember it.
...You've gotten rather direct lately. Fine, I'll remember that.
You're making this easy for me. All right, I'll get my life steady first.
I'll still come to sell goods. You don't have to ask me what happened every time.
I'm a regular. Ordinary customers don't know what you buy.
The next afternoon, two people come to the window, one behind the other. The first carries half a sack of secondhand goods.
We agreed I'd be the one to bring her! Then she starts running over here by herself every day — what does that make me?
It makes you the guide. I knew the way already.
Oh, listen to that mouth.
Just tell me—hasn't she been looking better lately? Face is a little rounder.
Whose face is round. Cut it out.
Lydia lifts her wrist and gives it a shake. The old bracelet glints under the light.
I wear the bracelet every day. When my family asks, I say I found it myself.
Oh, enough about the bracelet. I'm here to see her today.
My family's been going through my accounts lately. I have to be back before dinner. I got her here.
Next time I'll come on my own. I've got things to buy too. That's settled, then.
You two sure are close.
One bracelet's worth of friendship. I'm off!
Eleanor sets the sack on the counter. Metal parts clink inside; she takes her time untying it.
She talks a lot. Don't take it all seriously.
The room's registered now. Mother sleeps in the bed at the back.
She came here yesterday. After she got back, she didn't say a word to me.
She bought household goods, and something to eat.
That's all?
That's all. Paid the marked price.
...Fine. That's her, all right.
She opens the sack and tips out an old box, its lid split along a seam. And a roll of coiled wire.
The crack's in the lid. The bottom's fine. I measured the wire myself. Nothing broken.
Name your price.
Box goes as secondhand. Wire counts as a full roll.
About what I figured. A little less and I'd still take it.
She puts the coins in her purse, ties it twice, and stays at the window.
There's something we need to settle first. I haven't forgotten the crate from the man pretending to be my uncle.
You did make it right afterward, and you've told me things first ever since.
I'm willing to trust you again. But what you did that time was still wrong.
If there's danger from now on, I'll tell you first.
No goods today. There is something I want to tell you.
You always ask what's for sale first. Don't ask today.
I've been coming more often lately than when I had goods to sell.
I wonder whether you found anything good today, whether your lunch has gone cold again, whether you argued with another difficult customer.
Mother is safe now, and I still want to see you every day.
Eleanor, I feel—
Wait. Let me finish. I like you.
There. Your turn. Don't keep me waiting.
I like you too. It has nothing to do with where you used to live.
Nothing to do with where I lived? Easy for you to say.
Then when I needle you, don't dodge.
Good. Then I won't need an excuse to come here anymore.
I want to know you better. But can we take it slowly?
Yes. I'm not asking you to sign a lifetime contract today.
Just don't pretend you didn't hear me.
I care about you. But not that way.
I see.
You telling me directly is better than letting me guess.
You don't owe me for the past. And this isn't repayment.
I'll still come sell goods in a couple of days. Act normal then.
I said some harsh things before. I want to add one thing today.
I've been a lot of trouble lately. Thank you.
If there's something I can help with, come and find me.
The sky darkens and the streetlights come on one by one. She sits on the crate outside the window, tapping the ground with her toes.
We're closed.
I know. I'm not buying anything.
Mother's home. The guards just finished roll call. She'll cook her own nutrient fruit.
She pulled the pendant out by its cord, gripped it in her palm, then tucked it back.
Hey. I'm telling you something. Don't cut in.
When I first came down here, I thought every pawnshop in the lower district was the same.
That other place kept haggling me down and docking the purity. When they shorted me a few credits, I didn't come to you to make it up.
But I keep coming here. You're not cheap either.
What you did for my mother — I haven't forgotten.
Don't think I'm paying off a debt.
...I like you.
That's it. Do what you want.
The sky darkens and the streetlights come on one by one. She sits on the crate outside the window, tapping the ground with her toes.
We're closed.
I know. I'm not buying anything.
Mother's home. She can cook her own nutrifruit.
She pulled the pendant out by its cord, gripped it in her palm, then tucked it back.
Hey. I'm telling you something. Don't cut in.
When I first came down here, I thought every pawnshop in the lower district was the same.

What you did for my mother — I haven't forgotten.
Don't think I'm paying off a debt.
...I like you.
That's it. Do what you want.
The shopkeeper reaches through the window. She lifts her hand from her knee and lets him take it.
Me too.
You answered so fast. Those words took me three days.
I've thought about it longer than you.
Hah. Then why didn't you say it first?
You said not to make decisions for you.
...You remembered that too.
She didn't pull her hand back. She gripped his fingers instead, a little too hard.
Let's get this straight. I still scavenge. I still sell. You misprice, I'll still call you out.
I'm coming tomorrow. Even if I don't buy anything.
My mother — I'll tell her myself. Don't you go.
Okay.
She stands, lets go of his hand, and steps back to leave room for the window shutter.
Close up. I'll wait outside.
I think of you as a friend. And I will going forward.
...Got it. You said it clear. Saves me guessing.
I'll come tomorrow to sell. By the price tag — don't give up a single coin.
She stands, pushes the crate back beside the window, and leaves.
I saw a batch of goods you might want. I didn't agree to anything for you.
I asked where it came from, and what's broken. When the person arrives, you look for yourself.
Well? I picked well, didn't I?
I didn't hide the flaws. Praise my eye, not my character.
Not suitable? Then don't take it. You can turn down anything I bring.
I'll help you look next time too. But first I need to understand what I missed this time.
My mother says my tone when bargaining sounds more and more like yours.
She says at least now I know what I'm talking about.
I said the teacher is average. The student is the smart one.
Isn't a clever girlfriend like me enough?
You didn't argue with me this time. That counts as progress.
Teach the new ones to tell a rusted connector from a good one first.
Today I'm really here to buy something.
She was angry with me for speaking for her last time.
I apologized to her. She said don't just apologize to the owner. It makes it sound like she doesn't have a mouth of her own.
I saw her mother. Thinner than before. Still talks the same way, won't let anyone praise her too much.
I asked someone who knows about that bracelet. The price you offered was fair.
Tell that to people upstairs and they won't believe there's a shopkeeper like that down here.
Before, when we picked gifts, we only worried they weren't expensive enough.
This time she told me to bring things that are actually useful, not turn a visit into an exhibition.
She's right. It's the tone that makes it hard to admit right away.
She told me you're together. I don't have conditions to set.
When she said it, she wasn't planning to ask my opinion at all.
Word going around up there is that Eleanor has taken a liking to a pawnshop owner in the lower levels.
I deflected a few things for her. That was her trouble, not yours. Don't take it personally.
She says you're a friend worth keeping. She rarely uses the word 'worth.'
Whenever I try to sing her praises to her face, she tells me I talk too much.
If suitable business comes up in the future, I'll have people come talk to you directly. You won't owe me a favour.
If the goods are right and the price is right, we'll talk.
No wonder she says that all the time now.
My mother found a place willing to let her help organise equipment. Not her old farm, but she wants to go.
I'll help out for a few days first. I found steadier work too, so I won't have to rely on scavenging.
Someone from the research side came to ask if we'd help organise the records my mother left behind.
Some of the work is up there. It needs a separate work permit. It's not a return to our old life, and the case isn't closed.
My mother wants to keep doing research. I want to understand the parts I couldn't follow.
Of course I'm going. I didn't come here today to ask for your permission.
I came to work out the schedule with you.
I want to keep working, and I want to keep seeing you.
I'm not planning to drop the work, and I'm not planning to drop you.
Now I choose for myself. Don't start deciding 'what's good for me' again.
Say something when you're busy. Stop saying the shop can't spare you and then skipping proper meals.
I'd like coming here to be more than being a regular customer.
All right. I'll set aside the time. You have to set aside yours too.
I might not come as often in the future. But we can still help each other with business.
If you need anything, don't forget to come ask me.
That time you asked the price, I didn't sell it. Do you remember?
I told my mother I wanted to give it to you. She said it's mine, so I decide.
It's not for sale. You'd better have learned the difference by now.
Take it. Don't put it out with the stock. I'm not that generous.
Fine, I'll wear it myself. You'll see it anyway.
I originally wanted to give you that locket. In the end, I sold it to make up the money.
You don't need to find something else to replace it. I just wanted you to know I thought about it.
Hey. Got a moment today?
My mother's fine, and I still have my job.
You'll have to get used to it. I don't only show up when something's wrong.
My mother keeps telling me to bring an extra portion of food.
This one's for you.
The room's small, so we count every credit. Mother still has nightmares.
When she wakes up, I'm right there.
The first time I came here, I said this shop wasn't much. It still has plenty that needs fixing.
Don't think that because I like you, I like the broken lights too. My temper doesn't disappear just because I'm in love.
Let me stay a while today. If a customer comes, do your business.
If no one comes, talk to me.
Just don't start with 'how much more do you need?'
Come to me if you need something. Or if you don't.
You still haven't fixed that lamp?
My chipped cup still holds water. But you watched me pick a chipped one!
Mother made too much. She told me to bring you some.
Take it. Don't ask why there's always exactly one extra portion.
Ask too much and the cook won't know what to say. Eat.
I knew that customer just now. He used to tell me not to associate with people down here.

Don't waive this one today. I got paid.
I just wanted you to know I can take care of someone too.
Once you've finished the accounts, sit with me a while.
I sorted this batch. The bad ones are together. Don't say I didn't warn you.
I'm an old hand now. Don't bring up my first scavenging trip again.
All right, let's talk about today's price first.
Let's not talk about all that today. Got anything new in the shop?
Goods, not news. Preferably the kind where I can find a few things wrong.
Good. Sounds like an ordinary trip to the shop.

I told them about my mother too. They agreed to include the threats, but not to get her out.
I'll keep asking about her and left an address where they can find me.
You don't have to tell me we did the right thing.

The morning the paper came out, they killed my mother.

Don't tell me she would have wanted this. I can't ask her anymore.
I know there were other ways. I know why I didn't choose them.
But knowing that doesn't make this any easier.
I want to stay here for a while. Don't ask me if I want a drink.
They only returned a few of Mother's things.
A list she wrote. All little things about the farm.
Which light was broken, what tools were missing, which grow tank needed checking again.
Not every page is research that could change the whole station.
Most of the time, she was just busy with these things.
I'm keeping this list. It's not for sale.
Thank you. I'll take the food.
Life has to go on. I know. Just not that fast.
I joined the Revolution.

They'll help me make Pastel pay, and they can keep me out of the company's reach. The research can keep spreading too.
I asked what they're going to do. I won't agree to anything just because someone promises revenge for me.
I won't stay in the same place. I can't come here on a fixed schedule anymore.
I won't use your shop as a contact point. You helped me. That doesn't mean you should carry every risk from now on.
Sometimes, though, I might still need someone I can have an ordinary conversation with.
Of course I know where this place is.

Someone's teaching me. I'm not going to wave around something I can't use just to frighten people.
I'll check the condition first. I don't want anything broken.
I have enough money. Don't waive this one for me.
Then I'll look elsewhere. I'm not in a hurry to take something more likely to hurt me.
Before, all I wanted was to go back to how things were.
Now I can't even say what I want to become.
Don't take anyone's word too seriously. Including mine.
I'm looking for Eleanor. But she said not to ask around about where she lives.
I won't ask around. I'm not here to take her back, and I know how bad that would sound right now.
I just want to explain what her mother did for my family before. Back then, I did nothing for her.
When she's ready to listen, I'll tell her myself.
If she needs something normal that can be bought, I can help find it. I don't need to know where she goes.
Please pass that on to her.
I got Lydia's message.
Later. I don't have the energy to teach everyone how to talk to me right now.
I know there are things between us we never finished saying.
I care about you. That didn't disappear because something happened to my mother.

When I can come back, I will. I can't promise anything else right now.
I'll remember this place. Not just the research and the investigator's money.
I also remember the first time I turned my nose up at your cup. It really was chipped. I wasn't wrong about that.
I'm here for food for the road. We're leaving with the revolutionaries soon.
Nutrifruit too. Seeing it now makes me feel that at least some things weren't for nothing.
Pick out what I can carry. I'll pay the usual price.
I should go.
Take care of yourself. Don't take in every bit of trouble that comes to your door.
Thank you again. For everything. I hope next time we can talk about something else.
Where's Mother's research disk?

I asked you to keep it, not to decide what my mother is worth for me.
